props.title: They All Laughed

sections.content: Peter Bogdanovich's They All Laughed (1981) represents a pivotal moment in both screwball comedy evolution and New Hollywood's twilight. Following private detectives tracking potentially unfaithful wives in Manhattan, the film channels the spirit of The Lady Eve (1941) and Bringing Up Baby (1938) while incorporating the looser, more naturalistic style that defined 1970s cinema. The tragic murder of Dorothy Stratten shortly after filming cast a dark shadow over the production, leading Bogdanovich to personally distribute the film after studios backed away. This financial gamble ultimately bankrupted him, marking a dramatic turn in his career after earlier triumphs like The Last Picture Show (1971) and Paper Moon (1973).

sections.content: The film's New York setting becomes almost a character itself, captured with the same loving attention Woody Allen would bring to Manhattan (1979). Ben Gazzara, John Ritter, and Audrey Hepburn deliver performances that balance sophisticated comedy with genuine emotional depth. The surveillance plot allows Bogdanovich to explore themes of watching and being watched, creating a meta-commentary on cinema itself while maintaining the light touch required for romantic comedy. The influence of They All Laughed can be seen in later Manhattan-set romantic comedies like When Harry Met Sally (1989). SUBHEAD: The Last Great Screwball Comedy

As perhaps the final true screwball comedy of the classical style, They All Laughed represents both a celebration and eulogy for the genre. While films like What's Up, Doc? (1972) had previously attempted to recreate screwball's magic, Bogdanovich here updates the form for a more modern sensibility. The film's complex plotting and coincidence-driven narrative recall classics like The Palm Beach Story (1942), but its treatment of relationships and sexuality feels thoroughly contemporary. This bridging of classic and modern sensibilities would influence later romantic comedies like Broadcast News (1987) and The Truth About Cats & Dogs (1996).
